Notably, forward P/E (19.1x) is only mildly above its 10-year average — the Buffett Indicator's extremity is much more about mega-cap concentration than broad-market multiple expansion.

Implication: Friday's oil-driven rate shock (crude near $100) hit small-cap industrials hard — exactly SPXC's sector — while GOOG shrugged it off on company-specific news. Don't read one name's resilience as the market's; keep stops honest.

Note: direct Yahoo/currentmarketvaluation.com fetches were network-blocked this run (see footer); reading triangulated from GuruFocus and MarketCrash.net search snippets, not the primary source.

📰 Position News

Neither position has enhanced_news_watch set in portfolio.json — light-touch scan given both have standing action items above.

🔵 GOOG — Google Cloud backlog hit $514B (+82% YoY revenue growth reported), the main driver of the recovery from Sept 9's dip to Friday's $335.45 close. Analyst consensus target ~$415, implying ~24% upside from Friday's close. This is also the news that most plausibly explains why a stop at $333.90 wouldn't have stayed triggered for long even if briefly touched.

🟢 SPXC — No fresh company news this week; last catalyst was the late-July Q2 beat-and-raise (FY guidance: revenue $2.705–2.765B, adj. EPS $8.20–8.60). Friday's session saw a broad rotation out of small-cap industrials into oil producers (Russell 2000 −2.4% for the week) as crude approached $100 — a sector headwind, but irrelevant to the exit decision, which is about the Kranze defense-electronics segment, not fundamentals.

No fresh discovery candidate generated automatically here — that's what stock-finder is for. Not suggesting adding to either current position: GOOG's status needs IBKR verification first, and SPXC is actively being exited on the defense rule. With ~62% of the account sitting in cash and two open compliance/data questions, the priority is clearing those before deploying anything new. Your call.

📚 Today you learned

Real Rates and the Duration of a Growth Stock

Bond people call it duration: how much a security's price moves for a given change in the discount rate. Growth stocks behave the same way even though nobody prices them off a yield curve. Most of GOOG's value sits in cash flows 5-10+ years out — push the discount rate up, which is exactly what an oil-driven rate shock like Friday's does, and those far-out flows get hit harder than a slow-growing industrial's near-term cash. That's why crude approaching $100 hammered small-cap industrials (SPXC's sector, Russell 2000 -2.4% on the week) while high-multiple growth names felt it too — GOOG only shrugged it off because the Cloud-backlog beat was a bigger positive surprise the same session. The sensitivity didn't disappear, it just got out-run.

Also today: Discount rate — the rate used to convert a future cash flow into today's value; most growth-stock valuation arguments are really disagreements about which discount rate is correct.
